A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MoA research. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original mathematical and commonsense reasoning experiments, efficiency measurements, ablations, and expert-routing analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds Qwen3 experiments, HumanEval code-generation evaluations, and an expert-activation analysis.

M1.justification: The reported FFN LoRA placement changes from the up-projection to the down-projection in Figure 1 and Section 4.3, with corresponding expert-label updates. The expert types, sigmoid routing, learned threshold, and Soft/Sparse procedures remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish whether the placement revision reflects an implementation change or a documentation correction.

E1.justification: Appendix B.4 adds code generation, using CodeAlpaca-20k for training and HumanEval for evaluation. This introduces a distinct task domain beyond v1's mathematical and commonsense reasoning coverage, which is retained.

E2.justification: FlyLoRA joins the mathematical reasoning comparison in Table 1 and the new Qwen3 comparisons. The code-generation comparison also evaluates DenseLoRA and FlyLoRA. The existing LoRA/MoE comparator suite and the UniPEFT routing comparison are retained.

E3.justification: Evaluation expands from Llama3.1-8B to Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B. Appendix B.3 reduces MoLoRA, HydraLoRA, and AdaMoLE to four experts on Qwen3-14B following memory failures. Code evaluation introduces pass@1/5/10, validation-based checkpoint selection, five versus one training epochs for Qwen versus Llama, and a 500-token limit. Section 4.3 also revises the stated FFN target from W_up to W_down without establishing reruns.

E4.justification: Section 6.2 adds an AddSub analysis of inter-expert activation dispersion to investigate specialization versus redundancy. Existing component, threshold, routing-level, and case-study analyses remain. In particular, v1's threshold ablation moves from Section 5.2/Table 4 to Appendix B.1/Table 5.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-seed means and standard deviations for the main reasoning results and show the same seeds in routing plots. The new Qwen3 tables reuse this practice; no increased run counts or new uncertainty procedures are reported. Inter-expert activation dispersion is a diagnostic, not uncertainty about experimental estimates.

E6.justification: v2 adds FlyLoRA results, Qwen3 reasoning tables, HumanEval results, and activation-dispersion measurements. For example, Qwen3-14B mathematical averages are 86.40 for Soft MoA and 86.16 for Sparse MoA; Qwen3-8B HumanEval pass@1 scores are 50.61 and 50.30. Previously reported numerical entries are retained. These additions represent new comparisons and settings, not demonstrated same-setting performance gains between versions.

T1.justification: The method equations and Appendix A's mathematical formulations remain substantively unchanged. The new activation diagnostic uses the standard standard-deviation formula; it adds no theoretical derivation, theorem, proof, or formal assumption. Appendix A's input-variable correction is not a substantive mathematical revision.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about heterogeneous expert specialization, Soft/Sparse MoA, parameter efficiency, and computational performance. The additional experiments do not redefine these main contributions.

C2.justification: Section 6.2 newly interprets low activation dispersion as representation collapse and higher dispersion as specialization attributable to heterogeneity. Appendices B.3-B.4 add interpretations concerning generalization across model families and sizes, weaker sparse-MoE code performance, and FlyLoRA's variability across backbones. The explicit limitations section is unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 supplies FlyLoRA/DenseLoRA ranks and technical settings for the new model and code experiments; Figure 3 now identifies BoolQ. It removes v1's explicit batch size of 32 and two-GPU specification, retaining only A6000-48G hardware. Section 4.3 also introduces conflicting eight-expert and seven-expert descriptions of MoA. Project-access information is unchanged.

R1.justification: References to DenseLoRA, FlyLoRA, CodeAlpaca, and HumanEval are added for the expanded experiments. Section 2 and the central positioning of heterogeneous MoA against homogeneous MoE-LoRA remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 makes local wording, terminology, author, and contact-information edits. It moves the threshold discussion into Appendix B.1 and consolidates the instance-level routing discussion in B.2, followed by new experimental subsections. Most existing scientific prose and the main narrative remain intact.

P2.justification: The visual evidence expands through a specialization table, two Qwen3 benchmark tables, and a two-backbone code-generation table. Table 1 gains a comparator row, Table 3 receives clearer component labels, and the threshold table moves into the appendix. Figure 1 is revised and routing-figure labels change from up-projection to down-projection.

improvement.justification: The new model, code-generation, and comparator evaluations broaden the evidence beyond v1's single-backbone reasoning experiments. However, reporting weaknesses limit the gain: v2 removes training details, introduces inconsistent expert counts, and overstates consistent code-task superiority. Table 9, for example, gives Llama3.1-8B MoLoRA a pass@10 of 72.56 versus 70.73 for both MoA variants. Overall, the expanded evidence is useful, but clarity and interpretation do not improve consistently.
